strengths: The paper addresses an important, underexplored NLP/speech problem and usefully broadens audio chaptering beyond transcript-only formulations.

The comparison spans transcript models, handcrafted acoustic features, learned waveform representations, and multimodal LLMs on a large real-world dataset. The duration-, speaker-, ASR-, and failure-based analyses are informative.
The taxonomy of reference-, ASR-, hybrid-, and time-space evaluation protocols clearly exposes how transcript granularity and timestamp projection can affect reported results.
AudioSeg is conceptually simple and empirically promising, while the feature ablations provide credible evidence that pauses and speaker cues can complement transcript semantics.
The appendix supplies prompts, architecture and training hyperparameters, feature definitions, alignment procedures, and MLLM failure statistics, improving transparency.
weaknesses: The central claim that AudioSeg is superior to text-based systems is confounded by unequal output/evaluation discretization. AudioSeg is trained to predict the same 6-second grid used by T1, whereas text systems must first select sentence boundaries and then project them onto that grid. Table A5 explicitly shows only a 74–81% oracle F1 ceiling for these text pipelines, while the directly grid-trained audio model has no corresponding projection ceiling. Consequently, the raw 45.52 versus 40.30 F1 comparison does not isolate the value of audio representations. A matched output space, ceiling-normalized analysis, or continuous-time comparison is needed.

Although continuous-time protocol T2 is presented as the most direct and transcript-invariant formulation, no T2 results are reported and no temporal collar is selected or validated. The empirical protocol study is limited to T1 and several text-space variants, so a major stated contribution remains largely formal rather than demonstrated.

The strongest AudioSeg encoder is Whisper Large, which encodes substantial linguistic information and was trained on similar web audio. Calling the result evidence that audio provides information superior to text is therefore too strong without controls separating implicit linguistic content, acoustic cues, pretraining scale, and domain match.

Evidence lacks uncertainty estimates, multiple seeds, significance testing, and precision/recall or predicted-boundary-count diagnostics. Several highlighted gains are modest, so it is unclear which differences are robust.

The claim that non-speech cues explain AudioSeg's advantage is only weakly established. The cited examples are anecdotal, and DeepFilterNet can alter speech and other acoustic properties in addition to removing music or effects; the 2.21-point degradation is therefore not a clean causal ablation.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful appendices: code and models are only promised, while data split details, random seeds, decision-threshold selection, checkpoint selection, several preprocessing/decoding settings, and full compute requirements are absent. Evaluation also relies on default segeval parameters without establishing that defaults are appropriate for a 6-second time grid.

All evidence comes from one English YouTube dataset, and performance collapses on long recordings—the use case most associated with chaptering. This substantially limits the generality and practical impact of the conclusions.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and relatively underexplored speech/NLP problem, and its comparison of transcript-based, audio-only, and multimodal approaches is broader than prior work on audio chaptering.
The explicit separation of text-space and time-space evaluation exposes a genuine comparability problem when systems use different transcripts or sentence segmentations.

The empirical study is substantial: it covers multiple speech encoders and ASR conditions, handcrafted-feature ablations, MLLM prompting and adaptation strategies, and breakdowns by duration and speaker composition.
The architecture, prompts, feature definitions, and many training hyperparameters are documented clearly, and the MLLM failure analysis is particularly informative.
weaknesses: The headline claim that AudioSeg is superior to text-based methods is not established by a modality-controlled comparison. AudioSeg may select any 6-second cell and is evaluated directly on that grid, whereas text systems are restricted to sentence boundaries and then incur forced-alignment and projection errors. The reported oracle ceiling of only 73–81% confirms this systematic disadvantage. A matched text-on-time-grid baseline, or evaluation after restricting all systems to the same candidate boundaries, is needed.

The proposed time-based evaluation is insufficiently validated. All principal results use one arbitrarily anchored 6-second discretization, without sensitivity analysis over grid width or offset. Exact-bin F1 can change discontinuously near cell boundaries, while the continuous-time T2 protocol proposed by the paper is never evaluated. Ranking consistency is demonstrated only for three closely related MiniSeg variants and therefore does not validate cross-paradigm fairness.

There are no confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-seed results. Consequently, modest differences, feature gains, encoder rankings, and subgroup conclusions cannot be distinguished from optimization or sampling variation. Test-set sizes for the reported duration and speaker strata are also absent.

The non-speech ablation does not validate the claimed causal role of music and sound effects. DeepFilterNet can distort speech and alter the encoder's input distribution in addition to suppressing non-speech content, so the resulting 2.21-point decrease is confounded.

Several MLLM conclusions are similarly confounded. Predicted transcripts are forced-aligned for evaluation, while strategies differ dramatically in WER, transcript length, and generation failures. Thus the transcript-versus-transcript-plus-audio comparison does not isolate complementary segmentation information from improved transcription or alignment. These experiments are also restricted to recordings under 30 minutes.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: code and AudioSeg are only promised for future release, and the paper omits random seeds, decision-threshold selection, detailed split sizes, checkpoint-selection procedures, and some preprocessing and inference details needed to reproduce the reported comparisons.

The study uses only one English YouTube dataset, and its strongest encoder was pretrained partly on similar web audio. Together with the sharp degradation on recordings longer than 30 minutes, this substantially limits the generality of the conclusions.

Overall, the paper contains promising experiments and a useful problem formulation, but the unmatched output spaces and under-validated evaluation protocol directly affect its central superiority claim. These concerns prevent a clear Findings recommendation in the present form, though they appear addressable in a focused revision.

strengths: The paper makes a coherent, relevant contribution by reframing audio chaptering beyond transcript-only systems and comparing text-based, audio-only, and multimodal approaches within one study.

AudioSeg produces a substantial empirical gain: the Whisper-Large variant reaches 45.52 F1, compared with about 40 F1 for the strongest transcript-based variants. Its shared document encoder and transcript-free inference make this a meaningful result, even though the encoder itself was pretrained for ASR.

The experiments are unusually broad and informative. Feature ablations identify pauses as the principal hand-crafted acoustic cue; stratified analyses expose degradation with duration and multiple speakers; multiple audio encoders are compared; and the MLLM failure analysis reports instruction-following, looping, WER, and transcript-completeness problems rather than only aggregate scores.

The distinction among reference-transcript, ASR-transcript, aligned-text, discrete-time, and continuous-time evaluation clarifies an important methodological problem. The oracle experiment usefully quantifies the loss caused by snapping temporal boundaries to sentence units.

The architecture, feature extraction, prompts, and main hyperparameters are described in considerable detail, and the authors commit to releasing code, AudioSeg, and derived annotations. The work is clearly written and directly relevant to speech and NLP.
weaknesses: The strongest conclusion—that audio-only modeling is superior to text-based chaptering—is not fully isolated experimentally. AudioSeg uses the very large Whisper-Large ASR encoder, which encodes substantial lexical information and was pretrained on YouTube-like data, while the text baseline uses MiniLM. Thus the comparison conflates modality, encoder capacity, pretraining objective, and possible domain match. Calling inference transcript-free is accurate, but attributing the gain specifically to audio information is less secure.

The proposed evaluation framework is only partially validated. T2, the most direct continuous-time protocol, is formalized but not used in the reported comparisons; its collar width and boundary-matching procedure are also unspecified. The claim that T1 preserves rankings rests on only three closely related MiniSeg variants and F1 results, so it is not yet strong evidence of general ranking stability across model families.

There are no confidence intervals, significance tests, or multi-seed results. This limits confidence in smaller conclusions, including gains from most hand-crafted features and the 2.21-F1 DeepFilterNet ablation. Speech enhancement can also alter speech representations, so that ablation suggests but does not by itself validate the claimed role of non-speech cues.

Reproducibility has gaps despite the extensive appendix: the paper does not clearly report random seeds or variance, AudioSeg inference and threshold-selection details, which encoder layer or representation is extracted, complete compute requirements, or sufficient dataset-split information. The promised release mitigates but does not presently resolve these omissions.

All evidence comes from one English YouTube dataset with creator-provided chapter boundaries. The paper does not assess annotation reliability or cross-domain generalization, and performance collapses on recordings longer than 30 minutes—the setting where automatic chaptering is arguably most valuable. MLLM results are additionally restricted to shorter recordings and require a harder output task than the discriminative baselines.

The paper is sound and potentially suitable for the main conference, but the modality confound, limited validation of the proposed protocols, and lack of uncertainty estimates prevent a confident Conference recommendation. These issues do not undermine the core Findings-level contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses an important, underexplored NLP/speech problem and makes a coherent case that transcript-centric chaptering and evaluation omit relevant acoustic and temporal information.

The comparison spans text models, hand-crafted acoustic augmentation, an audio-only architecture, and multimodal LLMs. The consistent advantage of Whisper-based AudioSeg over the evaluated text systems is substantial, while the duration- and speaker-stratified analyses expose meaningful limitations rather than relying only on aggregate scores.

The formal distinction among reference-text, ASR-text, discrete-time, and continuous-time evaluation is clear and useful. The oracle analysis, granularity checks, and continuous-time collar evaluation provide good evidence that transcript choice and sentence discretization can distort comparisons.

Ablations identify pauses as the principal useful hand-crafted cue and provide some evidence for non-speech information through speech-enhancement filtering. The extensive appendices include prompts, feature extraction procedures, hyperparameters, failure analyses, and multiple evaluation variants.
The work is relevant to ACL and appears sufficiently sound for Findings; its combination of methodology, modeling, and empirical analysis also creates a credible case for main-conference publication.
weaknesses: The paper repeatedly interprets AudioSeg's advantage as evidence that audio captures information beyond transcripts, but the strongest encoder is Whisper Large, an ASR-pretrained model that encodes substantial linguistic content. The comparison establishes transcript-free inference, not that acoustic information itself explains the gain. Controlled experiments using matched-capacity semantic and acoustic representations, shuffled or masked speech content, or text-audio fusion are needed for the stronger mechanistic claim.

The empirical superiority claim is broader than the baseline evidence supports. The main supervised text comparator is MiniSeg, while stronger recent long-context chaptering or segmentation systems are discussed but not evaluated. AudioSeg also uses a much larger pretrained backbone, so the experiments do not isolate modality from model capacity, pretraining data, or possible YouTube-domain overlap.

Statistical reliability is insufficiently documented: results appear to come from single runs, with no confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance across seeds. This is especially problematic for small differences in the feature and protocol analyses, and for AMI, whose reported test sets contain only 16 meetings overall and just four under 30 minutes.

The claimed cross-domain validation is weak. The AMI experiment is very small, its annotation and adaptation procedure is underspecified, and the YTSeg-to-AMI models appear to be further trained on AMI rather than evaluated zero-shot. It therefore demonstrates transfer initialization more than broad domain generalization.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the extensive appendix. The manuscript does not clearly state the YTSeg split sizes and construction, random seeds, decision thresholds and model-selection procedure, AudioSeg compute requirements, or several preprocessing and truncation details. The asserted public release is not concretely accessible from the manuscript.

The proposed title evaluation is only a limited diagnostic: temporal matching excludes unmatched chapters and thus can report high title similarity on a very small matched subset, while global concatenation conflates title content, ordering, and chapter count. These measures do not strongly substantiate title-quality claims.

The main findings are much weaker for long recordings—the motivating setting—with severe degradation beyond 30 minutes and very low performance at 60 minutes or more. MLLM results are also largely restricted to recordings below 30 minutes. This limitation should constrain the paper's broad framing of long-form audio chaptering.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored NLP problem and usefully broadens audio chaptering beyond transcript-only pipelines.
The taxonomy of reference-, ASR-, and time-space evaluation protocols is clear and exposes a genuine comparability problem caused by transcript-dependent sentence segmentation.

The empirical study is unusually broad, covering multiple acoustic representations, handcrafted features, ASR conditions, multimodal LLM strategies, duration and speaker regimes, and limited out-of-domain evaluation.

AudioSeg is conceptually straightforward, and the appendix reports many architectural, training, prompting, feature-extraction, and evaluation details. The inclusion of continuous-time collar evaluation and multiple temporal granularities is valuable.

Several conclusions are appropriately nuanced: pauses dominate the handcrafted-feature gains, performance deteriorates on long recordings, and current MLLMs have serious instruction-following and temporal-grounding limitations.
weaknesses: The headline claim that audio-only modeling is superior to text-based modeling is not established by a controlled modality comparison. AudioSeg uses the large Whisper ASR encoder, whereas the main text baseline uses much smaller MiniLM representations and an older architecture. Differences in model capacity, pretraining data, semantic representation quality, and possible YouTube domain overlap are therefore confounded with the presence of audio.

The comparison also favors AudioSeg in output space. AudioSeg can place boundaries on every 6-second grid point, whereas text systems can predict only at sentence boundaries and consequently have an oracle F1 ceiling of roughly 74–81%. Time-space scoring removes dependence of the metric on a transcript, but it does not remove this difference in each model's candidate-boundary resolution. A controlled comparison that snaps all systems to the same candidates, or equips text models with a common time-grid prediction head, is needed.

The claim that AudioSeg captures structural information beyond transcripts is stronger than the evidence. Whisper is explicitly trained for ASR and can encode substantial linguistic content. The DeepFilterNet result is not a clean ablation of non-speech information because enhancement may distort speech and change the input distribution; the small 1.5–2.2 F1 decrease cannot by itself validate the proposed causal explanation.

Important empirical controls are missing: there are no multiple-seed results, confidence intervals, significance tests, or development-set selection details. This is particularly consequential for small differences among transcript variants and handcrafted features. The AMI evidence is too small for strong generalization claims, with only 16 test meetings and only four in the short-duration test subset.

The text comparison lacks stronger capacity-matched modern baselines. Zero-shot LLaMA and MiniSeg do not establish that the gain persists against a long-context text model trained under comparable parameter, data, and optimization conditions.

Some analyses are descriptive rather than identifying the claimed factor. Duration, boundary density, speaker composition, genre, and training frequency vary together, so the duration and speaker plots cannot support causal explanations without matched or multivariate analysis.

Title evaluation is weak: temporal matching excludes unmatched chapters and can yield high title scores from a very small matched subset, while global concatenation does not test whether individual titles describe the correct temporal content. The reported automatic lexical metrics, without human assessment, are insufficient to substantiate title-quality conclusions.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the stated code release and appendix: the paper does not report run-to-run variability, prediction-threshold selection, full split counts, exact encoder-layer extraction choices, or sufficiently precise implementation details for several settings. Overall, the work contains promising and potentially sound components, but the central superiority claim and 'fair comparison' framing require important controlled experiments before a clear Findings recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored NLP/speech problem: structuring long-form audio for navigation. Its comparison of transcript-based, audio-only, and multimodal approaches is broad and well motivated.

AudioSeg provides a practically useful transcript-free formulation and achieves a substantial empirical improvement over the reported text-based systems on YTSeg (45.52 versus 40.30 F1). The result is supported by multiple audio encoders and remains strongest under both discrete-time and continuous-time evaluation.

The formalization of reference-transcript, ASR-transcript, alignment-based, discrete-time, and continuous-time protocols is valuable. The oracle and granularity analyses convincingly expose problems with transcript-dependent evaluation and support time-based comparison.

The study includes unusually extensive diagnostics: ASR quality, acoustic-feature ablations, duration and speaker stratification, MLLM failure analysis, temporal grounding, title generation, non-speech filtering, and an out-of-domain AMI experiment.

The finding that pauses drive most gains from handcrafted acoustic features is clear and actionable. Results also identify meaningful limitations of current MLLMs, particularly context length, instruction following, and timestamp grounding.

The manuscript is clearly organized and supplies prompts, feature definitions, major hyperparameters, and alignment procedures. The stated release of AudioSeg and the evaluation toolkit further supports reproducibility.

Overall, the work appears sound and readily suitable for Findings; its breadth, practical relevance, and evaluation contribution also make a credible, though not decisive, case for the main conference.
weaknesses: The central conclusion that audio representations are superior to text is not cleanly isolated. The strongest AudioSeg system uses Whisper Large, a large ASR-pretrained encoder containing substantial linguistic information, while the principal text baseline uses the much smaller MiniLM-based MiniSeg. The gain may reflect encoder scale, pretraining, or domain match rather than an inherent advantage of audio. Stronger or capacity-matched text baselines and learned audio-text fusion would materially strengthen this claim.

No multi-seed results, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. This is especially important for the roughly five-point principal improvement, the smaller acoustic-feature gains, and the highly stratified analyses.

The cross-domain evidence is too small for strong generalization claims: AMI has only 16 test meetings overall, and the under-30-minute analysis uses four test meetings. Results lack uncertainty estimates, and the exact meaning and procedure of the YTSeg-to-AMI pretraining condition are insufficiently specified.

The DeepFilterNet intervention does not fully validate the claim that non-speech cues cause AudioSeg's advantage. Speech enhancement can modify speech and acoustic boundary cues as well as remove music or effects, and the observed degradation is modest. A controlled cue annotation or more targeted ablation would be more persuasive.

Several analyses are observational and potentially confounded. Duration buckets also differ substantially in boundary density and speaker composition, while the speaker regimes may differ in genre and duration. The LOESS curves therefore do not by themselves establish duration or speaker composition as causal factors.

The MLLM transcript-plus-audio comparison does not isolate acoustic segmentation information because supplying audio also changes transcript quality. The reported advantage demonstrates utility of audio to the end-to-end system, but not necessarily complementary boundary cues.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete despite the extensive appendix: dataset split sizes and seeds, number of runs, decision thresholds, checkpoint-selection criteria for most models, AudioSeg training compute, exact encoder-layer representation, and some decoding settings are not clearly reported.

The main-conference case is limited by modest architectural novelty and by overstatement of some conclusions. The strongest contribution is the systematic study and evaluation framework, while the evidence does not yet conclusively establish that transcript-free audio is intrinsically better than comparably strong text-based modeling.
